messages.author: b6fd2925353976cd
messages.subject: Warning messages
parts:
I know this has been discussed before on this list, but I would like to know when exactly I should start worrying about this kind of message:

"Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Invalid value of Sigma_subj: Error in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: Sigma_subjSigma_subj is not positive definite. Sigma_subj(0,0) is 8.63904e+06:0.
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified."

Perhaps the wording should be improved. It says "If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices,", but "sporadically" is a temporal adverb, but the example is given of a situation (when we have a covariance matrix). What does sporadically mean here? How do I decide that the warning is sporadic? I currently get this during the warmup phase.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Warning messages
parts:
Technically, you want to worry when your chains don't mix well.
Diagnosing non-mixing is another matter. One test that can be
done within Stan is to run with higher acceptance rate targets (delta
parameter), which will force smaller step sizes and increased numerical
stability, and make sure you get the same answer. Just be warned that
smaller step sizes are proportionally slower in NUTS.

You can also start warmup with smaller step sizes, which may eliminate
these messages.

Informally, if the problem goes away during warmup and only occurs
occasionally (or infrequently, or pick your own temporal adverb that
means not very often) during sampling. We don't have precise numbers for
this, but I'd be worried if you had the warning more than once every few
dozen iterations during sampling.

For efficiency and arithmetic stability, you almost never want to
use a covariance matrix variable. See the new section in the manual
chapter on regression for a fully Cholesky factored approach that is
both faster and more arithmetically stable than using covariance matrix
parameters.

- Bob

P.S. Temporal adverbs were a large part of my Ph.D. thesis
on the semantics intensional adverbs :-) I'm told there's a special
hell for semanticists (and probably for theory manglers --- I mashed
up Davidsonian event semantics and Montagovian intensionality).
